Real music, analysed by experts, with the Roman numerals under the notes where each chord begins. Each piece has **two analyses** by
different analysts, in tabs: compare them. They often agree, and where they don't, both readings can be defended. The analyses come from
[**When in Rome**](https://github.com/MarkGotham/When-in-Rome), a collection of harmonic analyses gathered by Mark Gotham and others.

**Reading the labels:** a key followed by a colon (`d:`) means the music has moved to that key (capital letter major, small letter
minor); the numerals after it are in the new key. The figures are those of [Chapter 16](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/FiguredBass.html)
(6, 64, 7, 65, 43, 42). ° is diminished and ø half-diminished, as in the book. `V/iv` and `vii°7/V` are the secondary chords of
[Chapters 17](secondary-dominants.qmd) and [18](secondary-diminished.qmd); `N6` is the [Neapolitan](neapolitan.qmd). A numeral sits
under the bass where its chord starts; where the bass holds a note through a chord change, the note is written as tied notes so the
label has a place (it sounds the same). **Resizing:** drag the line at the right edge of a score to make it wider or narrower (double-click
it to reset); the bars re-flow to fit, and the size is kept for every score on the page.

## Bach: "O Haupt voll Blut und Wunden" ("O Sacred Head, Now Wounded")

From the *St Matthew Passion* (BWV 244.54; no. 74 in Riemenschneider's collection of the chorales). Bach harmonized this melody several
times; this is one of them. Listen for the **key changes**: the phrases end in F, then D minor, then B♭ and G minor, then C and back to
F. Each new key is reached through its own dominant, as in [Chapter 22](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/Modulation.html). The
two analysts mostly agree. Where they differ, look at bars 6 and 7. In bar 6, one analyst reads IV64 where the other reads a cadential
6/4. In bar 7, one reads Imaj7 where the other reads I7.

{{< include _analysed-bach-o-haupt.qmd >}}

## Beethoven: Piano Sonata No. 14 in C♯ minor ("Moonlight"), I

The whole first movement (Adagio sostenuto). Triplets run under a slow melody throughout. The harmony changes slowly, usually once or
twice a bar, so this is a good piece for following an analysis by ear. Things to find:

- the **Neapolitan** (N6) in bar 3 and again later;
- the move to **E major** (the relative major) in bars 7–9;
- the long stretch of dominant harmony (V7 and i64 taking turns, bars 28–41) before the return;
- the **sections** the first analysis marks: exposition, development, recapitulation, coda.

{{< include _analysed-beethoven-moonlight-1.qmd >}}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## For teachers

- **Sources:** the analyses are When in Rome's RomanText files, CC BY-SA 4.0, shown as they are (signs written as in the book: ° ø, figures
  run together). The scores are Craig Sapp's Humdrum encodings of public-domain editions, converted to ABC by
  `scripts/when-in-rome/build.mjs`. That script also places each numeral at its bar and beat, and the browser test checks every
  converted note against the original encoding.
- **Notes and other readings:** where an analyst left notes or alternative readings in the file, they are listed under the score.
- **Not edited:** the analyses are not this site's, and some labels follow the analyst's conventions rather than the book's (Cad64, Imaj7,
  I7).
- **More pieces:** the corpus has hundreds more (all the Bach chorales, Beethoven's sonatas and quartets, 19th-century songs). The same
  script can add them.
:::
